chunks: My father narrated (may God be pleased with him) who said: Ahmad ibn Idris narrated to me who said: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab narrated to me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr al-Bazanty, from Umar ibn Azineh, from Bakir ibn A'yn, from Salim ibn Abi Hafsa, who said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying:

Indeed, the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) taught Ali (peace be upon him) one thousand chapters, each of which opens another one thousand chapters. So our companions went and asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about that, and it turned out that Salim had told the truth. Bakir said: And someone who heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) narrating this hadith narrated it to me, then he said: And not more than one or two of those chapters went out to the people. And most of my knowledge is that he said: Only one chapter.

key_terms.أَصْحَابُنَا: Our companions (referring to the Shia narrators)
key_terms.صَدَقَ: He told the truth (verifying the narrator's reliability)
key_terms.يَخْرُجْ إِلَى النَّاسِ: Goes out to the people (becomes public or widely known)
key_terms.يَفْتَحُ: Opens (indicating the depth or generative nature of the knowledge)

ai.seo_question: How much knowledge did the Prophet teach Ali according to this hadith?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Al-Khisal* highlights the concept of *Ilm al-Imam* (the Imam's comprehensive knowledge), illustrating that while Ali ibn Abi Talib possessed a vast, hierarchical reservoir of divine knowledge, the specific teachings revealed to the public were limited. This distinction underscores the Shia belief in the esoteric depth of the Prophet's family, where the majority of their knowledge remains hidden or specific to the Imams, contrasting with the limited exoteric revelation accessible to the general community.
